summary.text: The Calvin cycle is a series of chemical reactions in photosynthesis that converts carbon dioxide and hydrogen-carrier compounds into sugars.
In plants it takes place in the stroma of a chloroplast, using the ATP and NADPH made by the light-dependent reactions.
Though called the dark reaction, it does not occur in the dark, because it needs NADPH, which is short-lived and comes from the light-dependent reactions.

facts.label: Three phases
facts.value: Carboxylation, reduction reactions, and RuBP regeneration

facts.label: Direct product
facts.value: Three-carbon sugar phosphates called triose phosphates

items.prompt: A gardener says plants run the Calvin cycle at night, since it is called the dark reaction. What is wrong with that?

options.label: It needs chlorophyll to be absorbing darkness
It needs short-lived NADPH from the light-dependent reactions
It needs sunlight to warm the stroma first
It needs stored oxygen that builds up by day

items.explain: The cycle needs NADPH, which is short-lived and comes from light-dependent reactions, so it does not occur at night.

items.prompt: What does the Calvin cycle take from the light-dependent reactions to build sugars?

options.label: ATP for energy and NADPH for reducing power
Free oxygen and sugars that are already built
Light itself, which it captures in the stroma
RuBisCO and the thylakoid membranes themselves

items.explain: The cycle uses the chemical energy of ATP and the reducing power of NADPH from the light-dependent reactions.

items.prompt: The cycle's enzymes are switched on in light. What does this prevent?

options.label: The enzymes drifting out of the stroma into the cytosol
Six-carbon sugars piling up as the product
NADPH becoming even shorter-lived
The cycle being respired to carbon dioxide, wasting ATP

items.explain: Activation in light prevents the cycle from being respired to carbon dioxide, which would waste ATP with no net productivity.

items.prompt: Which molecules are the carbohydrate products that the cycle itself directly produces?

options.label: Six-carbon hexose sugars in a single step
Two-carbon groups that are passed on to mitochondria
Three-carbon sugar phosphates called triose phosphates
Five-carbon RuBP, which leaves the cycle as product

items.explain: The carbohydrate products of the Calvin cycle are three-carbon sugar phosphates, or triose phosphates, namely G3P.

items.prompt: Three carbon dioxide molecules go round the cycle and make six G3P. How many G3P does the cell gain, and why?

options.label: One, since five of the six are used to regenerate RuBP
Six, since all of them leave the cycle as product
Three, since each carbon dioxide leaves one behind
Two, since half are used up in making NADPH

items.explain: Of the six G3P, five regenerate RuBP, leaving a net gain of one G3P per three CO₂.

items.prompt: At night the Calvin cycle is not running. How do plants provide themselves with energy?

options.label: They run the cycle on NADPH stored from the day
They release sucrose into the phloem from starch reserves
They draw sugars up from the soil through the roots
They turn RuBisCO into a sugar-making enzyme

items.explain: In the dark, plants instead release sucrose into the phloem from their starch reserves to provide energy.
